fixes.explanation: Yes, friend. Paul says, “Brothers, I have conducted myself before God in all good conscience to this day.” Look at where he puts it: before God, not just before the council. That's a bold way to start when he's looking directly at the Sanhedrin.
Yes, friend. The text calls Ananias the high priest. He's the one who ordered those standing near Paul to strike him on the mouth. That's a heavy moment, and I think Paul felt it.

Not this one, baker. The commander is the one who brought Paul down and had the council assemble (Acts 22:30). The text calls Ananias the high priest, and he's the one who orders the strike. Two men with authority in one room, so I see how they got tangled.

Not in this scene, friend. The text never calls Ananias a centurion. It says the high priest Ananias ordered those standing near Paul to strike him on the mouth. The text gives him one title here, and it's high priest.

Not quite, baker. Later some scribes from the party of the Pharisees say, “We find nothing wrong with this man.” The split comes from what each group says about the resurrection. So the Pharisees aren't lined up against Paul over the law here.

Not this one, friend. The commander orders the soldiers to bring Paul into the barracks, not the temple. The commander was afraid they would tear Paul to pieces. So he ordered the soldiers to remove him by force.

Close, but no, baker. The text says the commander ordered the soldiers to bring Paul into the barracks. No palace in this scene. The dispute had grown so violent that he was afraid they would tear Paul to pieces.
